notes: The fourth day of Kislev, the ninth month would be December 7, 518 b.c., 22 months after the previous eight visions.

verses.zh: 那时伯特利人已经打发沙利色和利坚米勒，并跟从他们的人，去恳求耶和华的恩，
verses.en: Now the people of Bethel[NOTE:1] had sent Sharezer and Regem-Melech and their companions to seek the Lord’s favor
notes: For location see Map4-G4; Map5-C1; Map6-E3; Map7-D1; Map8-G3.

verses.zh: 并问万军之耶和华殿中的祭司和先知说：「我历年以来，在五月间哭泣斋戒，现在还当这样行吗？」

notes: This lamentation marked the occasion of the destruction of Solomon’s temple on August 14, 586 b.c., almost exactly 70 years earlier (cf. 2 Kgs 25:8).

verses.zh: 万军之耶和华的话就临到我说：
verses.en: The message of the Lord of Heaven’s Armies then came to me,

verses.zh: 「你要宣告国内的众民和祭司，说：『你们这七十年，在五月、七月禁食悲哀，岂是丝毫向我禁食吗？
verses.en: “Speak to all the people and priests of the land as follows: ‘When you fasted and lamented in the fifth and seventh[NOTE:1] months through all these 70 years, did you truly fast for me—for me, indeed?
notes: The seventh month apparently refers to the anniversary of the assassination of Gedaliah, governor of Judah (Jer 40:13-14; 41:1), in approximately 581 b.c.

verses.zh: 你们吃喝，不是为自己吃，为自己喝吗？

notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
The foothills (שְׁפֵלָה, shephelah) are the region between the Judean hill country and the Mediterranean coastal plain.

verses.zh: 耶和华的话又临到撒迦利亚说：

verses.zh: 「万军之耶和华曾对你们的列祖如此说：『要按至理判断，各人以慈爱怜悯弟兄。

verses.zh: 不可欺压寡妇、孤儿、寄居的，和贫穷人。谁都不可心里谋害弟兄。』」
verses.en: You must not oppress the widow, the orphan, the resident foreigner, or the poor, nor should anyone secretly plot evil against his fellow citizen.’[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “brother.” The Hebrew term ‘akh (אָח) may refer to a brother, relative, fellow countryman, or companion.sn Cf. Exod 22:21; Lev 19:33-34; Deut 10:18-19; 24:14, 17; 27:19.

verses.zh: 他们却不肯听从，扭转肩头，塞耳不听，
verses.en: “But they refused to pay attention, turning away stubbornly and stopping their ears so they could not hear.

verses.zh: 使心硬如金钢石，不听律法和万军之耶和华用灵藉从前的先知所说的话。故此，万军之耶和华大发烈怒。
verses.en: Indeed, they made their hearts as hard as diamond,[NOTE:1] so that they could not obey the law of Moses[NOTE:2] and the other words the Lord of Heaven’s Armies had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets. Therefore, the Lord of Heaven’s Armies poured out great wrath.
notes: The Hebrew term שָׁמִיר (shamir) means literally “hardness” and since it is said in Ezek 3:9 to be harder than flint, many scholars suggest that it refers to diamond. It is unlikely that diamond was known to ancient Israel, however, so probably a hard stone like emery or corundum is in view. The translation nevertheless uses “diamond” because in modern times it has become proverbial for its hardness. A number of English versions use “flint” here (e.g., NASB, NIV).
Heb “Torah”; the five books of Moses that make up the Pentateuch.

verses.zh: 万军之耶和华说：「我曾呼唤他们，他们不听；将来他们呼求我，我也不听！
verses.en: “‘Just as I[NOTE:1] called out, but they would not obey, so they will call out, but I will not listen,’ the Lord of Heaven’s Armies says.
notes: Heb “he.” Since the third person pronoun refers to the Lord, it has been translated as a first person pronoun (“I”) to accommodate English style, which typically does not exhibit switches between persons of pronouns in the same immediate context as Hebrew does.

verses.zh: 我必以旋风吹散他们到素不认识的万国中。这样，他们的地就荒凉，甚至无人来往经过，因为他们使美好之地荒凉了。」
verses.en: ‘Rather, I will sweep them away in a storm into all the nations they are not familiar with.’ Thus the land became desolate because of them, with no one crossing through or returning, for they had made the fruitful[NOTE:1] land a waste.”
notes: Or “desirable”; traditionally “pleasant” (so many English versions; cf. TEV “This good land”).

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible
Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible
for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the
Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Zechariah, chapters 7-8 form a literary unit. The theological issue is the Jews' covenant
faithfulness (cf. Zech. 7:9-13) vs. religious ritual (i.e. national fasting, cf. Zech. 7:3; 8:19).

- YHWH used the Jews' disobedience and subsequent dispersion for His own redemptive purposes
(cf. Ezek. 36:22-36; Romans 9-11). God will restore faithful Jews and welcome believing nations to Himself
(cf. Zech. 8:20-23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

- The promised covenant renewal still requires obedience (cf. Zech. 6:15 and 8:16-17). The covenant
requirements of the Old Covenant and the New Covenant are the same.

- repentance

- faith

- obedience

- perseverance

The Old Covenant was based on human performance, but the New Covenant is based on
a new heart, a new mind, and a new spirit from God (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36). However, both seek
a godly people to reveal YHWH's character to the nations whom He loves and desires that they know Him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT REQUIREMENTS OF ISRAEL

- New International Dictionary of Old Testament Theology and Exegesis, vol. 3, pp. 780-783

SPECIAL TOPIC: FASTING

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ZECHARIAH 7:1-7

1In the fourth year of King Darius, the word
of the Lord came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev.
2Now the town of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regemmelech and their men to seek the favor of the
Lord, 3speaking to the priests who belong to the house of the Lord
of hosts, and to the prophets, saying, "Shall I weep in the fifth month and abstain, as I have done these many years?" 4Then
the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying, 5"Say to all the people of the land and to
the priests, ‘When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months these seventy years, was it actually for Me that you
fasted? 6When you eat and drink, do you not eat for yourselves and do you not drink for yourselves? 7Are
not these the words which the Lord proclaimed by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was
inhabited and prosperous along with its cities around it, and the Negev and the foothills were inhabited?'"

7:1 "fourth year of King Darius" This is almost two years later than the initial eight visions
(cf. Zech. 1:1,7). The dating of this chapter is very specific.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF PERSIA

▣ "the word of the Lord came to Zechariah" This phrase introduces
a new revelation. It also seems to mark the paragraph divisions of this chapter. Zechariah did not choose
the time or subject. This is YHWH's message (cf. Zech. 7:4).

The Hebrew word dbr (BDB 182) is used regularly for God's revelation
(cf. Zech. 1:1,6,7; 4:6; 7:1,4,7,12; 8:1,18; 9:1; 11:11; 12:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "the fourth day of the ninth month" This would possibly be December 7,
518 B.C. (cf. UBS, A Handbook on Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, p. 180).

▣ "Chislev" This is a month in the Babylonian calendar (cf. Neh. 1:1), approximately November
or December.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE CALENDARS

7:2

NASB
"the town of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regemmelech"

NKJV, NRSV
"the people sent Sherezer with Regem-Melech"

TEV
"the people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and

Regemmelech"

NJB
"Bethel sent Sharezer"

JPSOA
"Bethel-sharezer and Regem-melech. . .sent"

Peshitta
"sent to Bethel Sherezar and Rab-mag, and the

king. . .had sent word to pray for him"

REB
"Bether-sharezer sent Regem-melech"

The Hebrew is very ambiguous. There are several theories:

- King James translates "Bethel" as "the house of God," not a town

- RSV, TEV, NIV and JB have "Bethel," which is a cultic city about twelve miles north of Jerusalem
and the center of calf worship in Israel during 922-722 B.C.

- NEB combines "Bethel" and "Sharezer" into one name. Similar compounds using Sharezer are found in
Jer. 39:3, while compound names using Bethel are found in Babylonian documents and in the
Elephantine Papyri (cf. W. F. Albright, Archaeology and the Religion of Israel, p. 169)

- the term "Regemmelech" (BDB 920) means "the king's spokesman" in Ugaritic (the Syriac translation
has "Rab-mag," which was an official title, cf. Jer. 39:3,13), which implies that Darius or
influential Jews sent two men (JPSOA, Bethel-Sharezer and Regem-Melech).

▣

NASB
"to seek the favor"

NKJV, Peshitta
"to pray before"

NRSV, NJB, REB, JPSOA
"to entreat the favor"

TEV
"to pray for"

LXX
"to appease"

This is the INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT of the Piel stem
(BDB 318 II, KB 316), which denotes the cessation of hostility (cf. Dan. 9:13), as well as the presence
of YHWH's blessing and acceptance (cf. Ps. 119:59). This same VERB is used in Zech. 8:21-22
for what the nations will seek from Him.

Just a brief theological note about the meaning of this Hebrew VERB in
the Piel stem.

- C. H. Dodd, The Bible and the Greeks has asserted that this VERB stem implies
"expiation" not "propitiation."

- This has been refuted by George Eldon Ladd, Theology of the New Testament (which I highly recommend).

- Ladd's position is also affirmed by Leon Morris (see Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, 2nd ed., p. 828).

- both BDB and KB assert that in the Piel stem it denotes "appeasement" in Zech. 7:2; 8:21; Mal. 1:9

SPECIAL TOPIC: BASIC PROCEDURES FOR A BIBLICAL WORD STUDY

7:3 "speaking to the priests. . .the prophets" The priests would refer to those who had returned
from Babylon with Zerubbabel and Joshua or Ezra. It is uncertain to whom "the prophets" refers. Haggai
and Zechariah are the only ones known by name. I think both Joel and Obadiah were also early post-exilic
prophets. Whomever they were these emissaries came to the representatives of YHWH asking about the
continuance of a fast denoting the destruction of Jerusalem, now that the Jews had returned to Jerusalem.

▣ "Shall I weep in the fifth month" This refers to a national day of mourning (fasting) which
the Jews initiated to remember the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple (cf. 2 Kings 25). But now
that they were back in Judah and the temple was rebuilt, should they continue this annual fast?

▣

NASB
"abstain"

NKJV, REB
"fast"

NRSV, JPSOA
"practice abstinence"

TEV, NJB
"fasting"

Peshitta
"separating myself"

LXX
"the holy offering"

The term (BDB 634) in the Niphal means to "dedicate oneself to God," "treat with
awe," or "fast." In this context "fast" is best. Context determines meaning!

▣ "as I have done these many years" This again is an allusion to the 70 year prophecy of exile
by Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 25:8-11; 29:10; Dan. 9:2,24; Zech. 7:5).

7:5 "Say to all the people of the land" This is an idiom for the common, non-leadership (cf. Jer. 34:10;
Hag. 2:4) people of God's covenant promise (i.e., Jews). For a good discussion of the way this idiom
developed and changed through Israel's history see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel: Social Institutions,
vol. 1, pp. 70-72.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PEOPLE OF THE LAND

▣ "seventh month" This refers to another national fast day to remember the death of Gedaliah,
the Babylonian appointed Jewish governor (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:25; Jer. 40:1-41:3). I think that possibly the ambiguous terms in
Zech. 7:2 and the fast days commended (cf. Zech. 8:19) related to a delegation of Jews from Babylon to
Jerusalem to discuss the status of the official ritual calendar.

▣ "seventy years" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SEVENTY YEARS

▣ "was it actually for Me that you fasted" YHWH did not initiate these fasts and really they
were done out of self pity more than worship (cf. Isa. 1:11-12; 58:1-12). YHWH is the One who sent Assyria
(Isa. 10:5) and Babylon (Jer. 13:9).

7:6 "When you eat and drink" This is sarcasm. They were fasting and/or feasting for themselves, not
for YHWH (cf. Isa. 29:13; Col. 2:20-33).

7:7 "the former prophets" See note at Zech. 1:4.

▣ "when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous" This refers to the time before the Babylonian
exile. Nebuchadnezzar II conducted four deportations.

- 605 B.C. ‒ Daniel and his three friends

- 597 B.C. ‒ Ezekiel and 10,000 skilled Jews

- 586 B.C. ‒ Jerusalem and the temple destroyed and most of the
remaining population exiled

- 582 B.C. ‒ after the murder of Gedaliah the Babylonian military
returned and exiled everyone they could find

▣ "the Negev" This (BDB 616) refers to the uninhabited pasture land in southern Judea.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GEOGRAPHICAL DIVISIONS OF THE PROMISED LAND

▣ "the foothills" This is literally "shephelah" (BDB 1050), which refers to the coastal
plain along the Mediterranean.

At the time of Haggai and Zechariah neither of these geographical areas belonged to the
returned Jews under Cyrus II's edict. Zerubbabel only controlled a small area around the city of Jerusalem.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ZECHARIAH 7:8-14

8Then the word of the Lord
came to Zechariah saying, 9"Thus has the Lord of hosts said, ‘Dispense true justice and
practice kindness and compassion each to his brother; 10and do not oppress the widow or the orphan, the stranger or the poor;
and do not devise evil in your hearts against one another.'" 11But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and
stopped their ears from hearing. 12They made their hearts like flint so that they could not hear the law and the words which the
Lord of hosts had sent by His Spirit through the former prophets; therefore great wrath came from the
Lord of hosts. 13And just as He called and they would not listen, so they called and I would not listen,"
says the Lord of hosts; 14"but I scattered them with a storm wind among all the nations whom they
have not known. Thus the land is desolated behind them so that no one went back and forth, for they made the pleasant land desolate."

7:8 Is this a textual marker to designate a new context? Joyce Baldwin, in Tyndale Old Testament
Commentaries, "Haggai, Zecharian, Malachi," (p. 145), says it is an editorial addition that misunderstood the unity of the passage.

7:9-10 The prophets always direct the people back to their covenant responsibilities. They are
"covenant watch dogs"! Zechariah 7:9-10 go back to the Mosaic covenant and its social requirements.

As an example, the Ten Commandants have requirements towards God (which they had violated,
cf. Zech. 7:9-10). The blessings of God as well as the cursings of God are related to covenant fidelity
(cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-29). These requirements and guidelines for life were not new or surprising to these
returning Jews.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT REQUIREMENTS OF ISRAEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

7:9 "Dispense true justice" There is a word play between the NOUN CONSTRUCT (BDB 1048)
and the Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 1047, KB 1622). Covenant people are to treat each other
fairly (cf. Micah 6:8). This particular phrase refers to judicial discussions (e.g., Lev. 19:15; Deut. 1:16-17; Prov. 31:9;
Ezek. 18:8; 45:9), but has a wider implication of appropriate covenant relationships between all the members of God's
people. This very term is repeated in Zech. 8:16. Injustice offends God (cf. Hosea 4:1-6).

▣ "kindness" This word is hesed (BDB 338), the special covenant NOUN which
speaks of YHWH's longsuffering covenant loyalty (possibly best understood as family love). YHWH is a faithful,
loving God and He demands the same of His people. For a good discussion see New International Dictionary
of Old Testament Theology and Exegesis, vol. 2, pp. 211-218 and Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the OT, pp. 111-116.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS (hesed)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "compassion" The term (BDB 933) originally had a family orientation ("from the womb"). This
same term was used earlier in the angel's prayer to YHWH about not having "compassion" for Jerusalem. The two
terms, "kindness" and "compassion" are used in Dan. 1:9 to describe YHWH's graciousness to Daniel through
Nebuchadnezzar's overseer. As He treats us, we as His people should treat one another (cf. Phil. 2:5ff; 1 John 3:16).
Our attitudes and actions show to whom we belong!

7:10 "do not oppress the widow. . .the orphan. . .the stranger. . .the poor" The NEGATED
VERB (BDB 798, KB 897) is a Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE
sense. Justice without partiality is a recurrent theme of the book of Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 1:17; 10:17;
16:19; 24:14,17). YHWH defends the defenseless.

For an expanded discussion on YHWH's care for

- widows, see NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 413-415

- orphans, see NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 570-571

▣

NASB, JPSOA
"the stranger"

NKJV, NRSV
"the alien"

NJB
"the foreigner"

Peshitta
"the proselyte"

REB
"resident alien"

LXX
"the guest"

This is the Hebrew term (BDB 158) which denotes a resident alien. These were free people,
not slaves, but they had limited civil rights. YHWH was seen as their protector and defender as He was for
all socially deprived, powerless, and poor people (cf. Exod. 22:21-24; Deut. 10:18). A special third year tithe was
received locally to aid society's needy (cf. Deut. 14:28-29; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: TITHING).

For a good discussion of Israelite social order see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel: Social
Institutions, vol. 1, pp. 69-79.

▣ "do not devise evil in your hearts" This VERB (BDB 362, KB 359) is another
Qal IMPERFECT used as a JUSSIVE. This refers to legal procedures
(cf. Zech. 8:17) with an emphasis on proper attitude and motives. Treat others with respect as fellow
covenant partners. Evil is always self-centered; love is always others-centered!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

7:11-12 This is a series of four parallel phrases describing the attitudes of disrespect and
disobedience of YHWH's people.

- "they refused to pay attention"

- "they turned a stubborn shoulder" (cf. Neh. 9:29)

- "they stopped their ears from hearing" (cf. Jer. 5:21; 6:10; Ezek. 12:2)

- "they made their hearts like flint so that they could not hear"

- also note Ezek. 7:13a and compare Isa. 6:9-10

7:12 "They made their hearts like flint" This Hebrew term (BDB 1038 I; NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 167) refers to some kind of very
hard material like corundum or diamond (cf. Jer. 17:1). It is used as imagery here of the hardness of
the Jewish ancestors' hearts toward their God. This same image of hardness is used in a positive way in
Ezek. 3:9 for YHWH equipping the prophet to face strong opposition.

This is active refusal to listen and heed YHWH's word and will (the opposite of shema).
His people were in open, active, willful rebellion!

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS

▣ "sent His Spirit through the former prophets" This refers to the inspiration of the OT prophets
(cf. Zech. 1:4; 7:7; Neh. 9:20,30) by the agency of the Holy Spirit (cf. 1 Pet. 1:11; 2I Pet. 1:21; "the God
breathed" of 2 Tim. 3:16).

Often in the OT the Spirit is a way of referring to God (e.g., Ps. 139:7-8; Isa. 40:13;
60:10-11) or God's creative activity (e.g., Gen. 1:2). God energizes humans to perform tasks with His
strength and wisdom (e.g., Exod. 28:3; 31:3; 35:31,34; Jdgs. 3:10; 6:34; 11:29; 13:54; 14:6,19; 15:14).

The OT does not clearly reveal the NT concept of three divine persons with one eternal essence,
but it does begin to reveal a personal plurality in Deity. The problem is that plurality and monotheism are hard
to reconcile. The church is forced to articulate a triune unity because of the NT affirmations of:

- the Deity of Jesus

- the personality of the Spirit

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT

▣ "therefore great wrath came from the Lord of hosts" This willful
disrespect and disobedience caused the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 to become a reality (cf. Dan. 9:1-19).

This disobedience with its resulting wrath (cf. Zech. 7:14) caused the nations to misunderstand
YHWH and His redemptive purposes (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

7:13 "He called" YHWH called to them through the covenants, the Exodus, the temple, and the prophets
(cf. Hosea 11:2), but they would not obey!

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS

▣ "they called and I would not listen" Now the tables are turned! YHWH called and they would not
hear, now they call for His help, but He will not hear (cf. Isa. 1:15), not only because of their covenant
disobedience, but also their covenant hypocrisy (cf. Isa. 1:11-15). If they would truly repent, YHWH would
respond (cf. Isa. 1:16-20).

7:14 "I scattered" YHWH is in control of history! This refers to the Babylonian Exile.

This VERB (BDB 704, KB 762) is a Piel IMPERFECT. In the
ancient world a military defeat meant the defeat of the national god. Israel and Judah's defeat was not
because of YHWH's weakness, but their sin (cf. Daniel 9). It was YHWH who caused both the Assyrian
(cf. Isa. 10:5) and Babylonian exiles (cf. Jer. 13:9; 51:20-24).

▣ "the land is desolated" The covenant promises were rescinded (cf. Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29). The
Covenant has always been conditional on God's grace and an appropriate human response.

God brought desolation (cf. Jer. 4:6) so that He could bring restoration to a repentant
people. Judgment is an act of love (cf. Heb. 12:5-13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣

NASB
"no one went back and forth"

NKJV, LXX
"no one passed through or returned"

NRSV
"no one went to and fro"

TEV
"no one living in it"

NJB, REB, JPSOA
"no one came or went"

Peshitta
"without any one to pass through"

This unusual phrase is found only in Zech. 7:14 and 9:8. Zechariah is divided into two
literary units (chapters 1-8 and 9-14). This unusual phrase appears in both units and, thereby becomes
evidence for the unity of the book by one author.
